problems.title: Create a DataFrame from List
problems.notes: pd.DataFrame(data, columns=[...]) from a raw 2D list — the whole point is knowing the columns= kwarg exists instead of renaming after the fact

problems.title: Get the Size of a DataFrame
problems.notes: df.shape returns (rows, cols) as a tuple, not a DataFrame — the trap is reaching for len(df) + len(df.columns) when shape does both in one call

problems.title: Big Countries
problems.notes: boolean OR filter with df.loc[(cond1) | (cond2), cols] — parenthesize each condition or Python's operator precedence on | silently breaks the mask

problems.title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
problems.notes: chained boolean AND filter on two string columns; the canonical first pandas-interview problem, equivalent to the SQL version everyone already knows

problems.title: Invalid Tweets
problems.notes: df['content'].str.len() vectorises character counts across the column — never .apply(len) here, that's the anti-pattern this problem is designed to catch

problems.title: Patients With a Condition
problems.notes: str.contains(r'(^|\s)DIAB1') needs the regex anchor — a naive str.contains('DIAB1') also matches 'SADIAB100', which is the hidden failing test case

problems.title: Create a New Column
problems.notes: df['bonus'] = df['salary'] * 2 is a vectorised broadcast assignment — the entire lesson is that you never loop rows to derive a column

problems.title: Calculate Special Bonus
problems.notes: set a default column then overwrite a subset with df.loc[mask, 'bonus'] = ... — the two-step default-then-override pattern beats an np.where one-liner for readability under interview pressure

problems.title: Fix Names in a Table
problems.notes: str.lower().str.capitalize() chain — capitalize() alone does not lowercase the rest of the string, so skipping the lower() first is the classic bug

problems.title: Drop Missing Data
problems.notes: df.dropna(subset=['name']) — always scope dropna to the relevant column(s); an un-scoped dropna() silently drops rows for missingness anywhere in the frame

problems.title: Fill Missing Data
problems.notes: df['quantity'].fillna(0) — know fillna vs dropna is a business decision, not a syntax choice; the interviewer wants you to say why you'd impute here instead of dropping

problems.title: Drop Duplicate Rows
problems.notes: df.drop_duplicates(subset=['email'], keep='first') — keep='first' is the default but say it out loud, since keep='last' or keep=False change which row survives

problems.title: Count Salary Categories
problems.notes: bucket with df.loc + boolean masks, groupby().size(), then LEFT-MERGE onto a hardcoded 3-row category frame so zero-count categories still appear — groupby alone silently drops empty buckets

problems.title: Rename Columns
problems.notes: df.rename(columns={...}) returns a copy by default — forgetting inplace=True or the reassignment df = df.rename(...) is the #1 silent-no-op bug in real pipelines

problems.title: Change Data Type
problems.notes: df['grade'].astype(int) truncates rather than rounds a float — know the difference from .round().astype(int) before an interviewer asks about 73.9 becoming 73

problems.title: Reshape Data: Concatenate
problems.notes: pd.concat([df1, df2]) stacks rows and duplicates the index by default — reset_index(drop=True) is worth mentioning even though this test case doesn't require it

problems.title: Reshape Data: Pivot
problems.notes: df.pivot(index='month', columns='city', values='temperature') — pivot() requires unique (index, columns) pairs; if duplicates existed you'd need pivot_table with an agg function instead

problems.title: Reshape Data: Melt
problems.notes: pd.melt(df, id_vars=[...], var_name=..., value_name=...) turns wide quarterly columns into long rows — this is the pandas-native answer to 'unpivot this wide table' asked in almost every DS screen

problems.title: Number of Unique Subjects Taught by Each Teacher
problems.notes: groupby('teacher_id')['subject_id'].nunique() — nunique() collapses duplicate (teacher, subject, dept) combos in one call, no drop_duplicates() pre-step needed

problems.title: Classes With at Least 5 Students
problems.notes: groupby('class').size() then filter the resulting Series with a boolean mask — size() counts rows including NaN, count() does not; know which one this problem actually needs

problems.title: Group Sold Products By The Date
problems.notes: groupby('sell_date')['product'].agg(['nunique', lambda x: ','.join(sorted(x.unique()))]) — multi-aggregation with a lambda in the same .agg() call is the reusable trick, not two separate groupbys

problems.title: Monthly Transactions I
problems.notes: extract month with dt.to_period('M') or dt.strftime('%Y-%m'), then groupby(['month','country']).agg(count=..., sum=..., approved_count=(mask).sum()) — conditional counts inside groupby via a boolean-times-1 trick is the real skill tested

problems.title: Immediate Food Delivery II
problems.notes: find each customer's first order via groupby('customer_id')['order_date'].idxmin() then index back into the frame — idxmin returns the row label, not the value, a common off-by-concept mixup

problems.title: Department Highest Salary
problems.notes: compute per-department max with transform('max') then filter salary == that max — transform broadcasts the group result back to every row so you can compare without a separate merge

problems.title: Customers Who Never Order
problems.notes: customers[~customers['id'].isin(orders['customerId'])] — isin() plus the tilde negation is the pandas idiom for a SQL anti-join/NOT IN, no merge required

problems.title: Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier
problems.notes: pd.merge(employees, employee_uni, how='outer') then dropna(subset=['name']) — outer join preserves employees with no unique_id as NaN, which is what the null requirement is asking for

problems.title: Students and Examinations
problems.notes: pd.merge(students, subjects, how='cross') builds every (student, subject) pair before left-joining the actual exam counts and fillna(0) — cross join is the tool candidates forget exists

problems.title: Nth Highest Salary
problems.notes: drop_duplicates(subset='salary').sort_values(ascending=False).iloc[n-1] wrapped in try/except for out-of-range n — this is a parameterised function, not a fixed query, so the edge case (n > distinct salary count) is the actual test

problems.title: Rank Scores
problems.notes: df['score'].rank(method='dense', ascending=False) — method='dense' gives no gaps after a tie, matching SQL's DENSE_RANK; 'min' would leave a hole and is the wrong default here

problems.title: Method Chaining
problems.notes: df[df.weight > 100].sort_values('weight', ascending=False)[['name']] in one fluent chain — the explicit ask is to avoid intermediate variables, which is exactly the style production notebooks should use
